passages.text: Archaeologists excavating a 4,000-year-old settlement found grinding stones coated with residue from wild grasses but none from domesticated wheat, even though wheat was being farmed at the same time in villages less than a day's walk away. The settlement's storage pits held large quantities of acorns and wild seeds. Because shells and obsidian traded from those farming villages turned up throughout the settlement, the absence of wheat residue suggests that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the settlement's residents did not know that wheat could be farmed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the residents were in contact with farming villages but continued to rely on wild plant foods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the farming villages were founded after the settlement had been abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the residents used their grinding stones only to process acorns.

content.explanation: Traded goods from the farming villages show the residents were in contact with farmers, so they likely knew about wheat. Yet the grinding stones and storage pits show only wild foods. The most logical conclusion is that they kept relying on wild plants despite that contact.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The trade goods show regular contact with wheat-farming villages, which makes it unlikely the residents were unaware of farming.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The text says the villages were farming wheat at the same time the settlement was occupied.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The grinding stones had residue from wild grasses, so they weren't used only for acorns.

passages.text: To find out why some loaves of their bread were collapsing, bakers at a small shop prepared two batches of dough with identical ingredients and baked them at the same oven temperature. The first batch rose for one hour before baking and the second for three hours. Only loaves from the second batch collapsed in the oven. Because the batches differed in only one way, the bakers concluded that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the oven temperature was too high for this kind of bread.

choices.label: B
choices.text: some of the ingredients had spoiled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: one hour was too short a time for the dough to rise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the longer rising time was likely causing the loaves to collapse.

content.explanation: The only difference between the batches was rising time, and only the batch that rose for three hours collapsed. So the longer rising time is the likely cause (choice D).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Both batches were baked at the same temperature, yet only one collapsed, so temperature can't explain the difference.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Both batches used identical ingredients, so spoiled ingredients would have affected both.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The one-hour loaves didn't collapse, so nothing suggests that rising time was too short.

passages.text: Biologist Amara Osei placed motion-triggered cameras throughout a city park to study red foxes. Over a full year, the cameras recorded foxes almost entirely between midnight and dawn, even though rabbits and other prey animals were active in the park at all hours. Osei also noted that the park was busy with people and dogs from early morning until late evening. These observations suggest that the foxes ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: hunt only animals that are active at night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: are active at times when they are least likely to encounter people and dogs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cannot see well in daylight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: find most of their food outside the park.

content.explanation: Prey was available all day, so food timing doesn't explain why foxes appear only after midnight. The other detail given is that people and dogs fill the park from morning to late evening. Foxes active only when the park is empty are likely avoiding people and dogs (choice B).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says prey was active at all hours and doesn't say foxes hunt only nighttime animals.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text concerns the foxes' eyesight.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says nothing about where foxes find food.

passages.text: Historian Grace Achterberg examined shop records from a river town before and after its only bridge was destroyed by a flood in 1871. The flood did not damage any shops, the number of people living on each bank changed little in the following years, and before the flood, shops on both banks had similar sales. During the six years it took to rebuild the bridge, sales at shops on the east bank, where most residents lived, stayed steady, while sales at shops on the west bank fell by more than half. This pattern suggests that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the flood caused more damage on the west bank than on the east bank.

choices.label: B
choices.text: shops on the east bank raised their prices after the flood.

choices.label: C
choices.text: many customers of west-bank shops had been east-bank residents who crossed the bridge to shop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: most west-bank residents moved to the east bank after the flood.

content.explanation: Most residents lived on the east bank, and only west-bank sales fell once the bridge was gone. The likely explanation is that west-bank shops had depended on east-bank residents who could no longer cross the river (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says the flood didn't damage any shops.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text concerns prices, and east-bank sales stayed steady.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says the number of people living on each bank changed little after the flood, so residents did not move from one bank to the other in large numbers.

passages.text: The nectar of a certain desert shrub contains a bitter compound in concentrations too low for bees to taste. In laboratory experiments, entomologist Rhea Castellanos found that bees fed nectar containing the compound were more likely than other bees to return to the same flower scent days later. Because a plant benefits when bees carry pollen between flowers of its own species, Castellanos's findings suggest that the compound ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: may help the shrub by making bees more likely to keep visiting its flowers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: discourages bees from visiting the shrub because of its bitter taste.

choices.label: C
choices.text: protects the shrub's nectar from drying out in desert heat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: makes the shrub's nectar taste better to bees than other nectar does.

content.explanation: Bees given the compound were more likely to return to the same scent, and the shrub benefits when bees move pollen among its own flowers. So the compound likely helps the shrub by encouraging repeat visits (choice A).

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The compound is too dilute for bees to taste, and it made them more likely to return, not less.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text links the compound to keeping nectar moist.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Bees can't taste the compound at these concentrations, so it can't make the nectar taste better to them.

passages.text: For decades, a portrait in a regional museum was assumed to be a copy of a more famous painting in a national collection. When conservators examined it with infrared imaging, they found an underdrawing beneath the paint in which the sitter's head faced a different direction and the hands had been redrawn several times. Copyists typically reproduce a finished composition directly, without such changes. The imaging therefore suggests that the regional museum's portrait ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: is a copy of a different painting from the one in the national collection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: was damaged and then repainted by later conservators.

choices.label: C
choices.text: was painted from memory by someone who had once seen the famous version.

choices.label: D
choices.text: may be an original work in which the artist was still working out the composition.

content.explanation: Copyists usually reproduce a finished design without changes, but this portrait's underdrawing shows the artist changing the head and redrawing the hands. That is what an artist does while developing a composition, so the portrait may be an original rather than a copy (choice D).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The evidence counts against the portrait being a copy at all, not in favor of it copying something else.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The changes are in the underdrawing beneath the paint, made while the work was created, not later repairs.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text points to painting from memory, and repeated reworking of the design fits an artist developing a composition better than someone copying.

passages.text: When a city library began lending e-books, some staff members worried that people would stop borrowing printed books. These findings suggest that the e-book program ______

choices.label: A
choices.text: caused a gradual decline in print borrowing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: attracted new library users rather than drawing existing borrowers away from print books.

choices.label: C
choices.text: was used mostly by people who had previously borrowed many printed books.

choices.label: D
choices.text: will eventually replace the library's collection of printed books.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Most e-book borrowers had no library card before, so they weren't previous print borrowers.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text supports predicting that print books will be replaced, and print loans held steady.

passages.text: Many rivers and hills in a mountain region have names that come from a language no longer spoken there. The region's town names, however, come almost entirely from the language spoken there today. Linguist Tobias Renn notes that names for natural features tend to last for centuries, because newcomers to an area usually adopt the names already in use for them. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: speakers of the older language once lived in the region, and most of its towns received their present names after speakers of today's language arrived.

choices.label: B
choices.text: speakers of the older language never lived in the region but named its rivers and hills from a distance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the newcomers renamed the region's rivers and hills but kept the existing names of its towns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the older language and today's language are closely related.

content.explanation: Rivers and hills carry names from the older language, and Renn explains that newcomers usually keep existing names for such features, so the older language's speakers were likely there first. Town names, by contrast, come from today's language, which suggests the towns got their names after the newer speakers arrived. Choice A combines both points.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Names that newcomers adopt from people already living there point to the older language's speakers having lived in the region.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This reverses the evidence: the rivers and hills kept older names, while the town names are from today's language.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text gives no information about how the two languages are related.

passages.text: On a chain of islands, populations of one lizard species differ in an unexpected way: lizards on islands with ground-hunting predators have shorter legs than lizards on predator-free islands. Longer legs help lizards sprint across open ground, while shorter legs help them grip narrow branches. Ecologist Farah Leclerc observed that on the islands with ground-hunting predators, the lizards spend most of their time high in shrubs. If her observations are accurate, the shorter legs most likely ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: allow these lizards to outrun ground-hunting predators across open ground.

choices.label: B
choices.text: show that predators have little effect on where lizards spend their time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: suit a life spent climbing in vegetation, a habit that keeps the lizards away from ground-hunting predators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: developed because the predators prefer to hunt lizards in shrubs.

content.explanation: The pattern seems surprising because longer legs would help a lizard sprint away. But Leclerc found that lizards on predator islands live high in shrubs, and shorter legs help with gripping branches. So the shorter legs fit a climbing lifestyle that keeps the lizards out of reach of ground hunters (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says longer legs, not shorter ones, help with sprinting on open ground.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Lizards behave differently on islands with predators, spending their time in shrubs, so predators do seem to affect where they live.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The predators are described as ground hunters, so it doesn't follow that they prefer hunting in shrubs.

passages.text: Account books from a medieval monastery record both the grain it harvested each year and the grain it gave to the poor. Historian Ruth Calloway found that in years of poor harvests, the monastery gave away more grain, not less, even though it had less to spare. In those same years, it also bought extra grain from distant markets at high prices. Some historians have argued that monastic charity was mainly symbolic, a token gesture that cost little. Calloway's findings suggest that, at least for this monastery, ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the view that monastic charity was mainly symbolic is accurate for most other monasteries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the monastery gave grain to the poor only in years of poor harvests.

choices.label: C
choices.text: charity was a substantial commitment that the monastery kept up even when doing so was costly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: poor harvests made the monastery wealthier by raising the price of grain.

content.explanation: The monastery gave away more grain in bad years and paid high prices for extra grain at the same time. Charity that grows when resources shrink and requires costly purchases is not a cheap token gesture; it was a real commitment kept up at significant expense (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Calloway's findings concern one monastery and say nothing about whether the symbolic view holds elsewhere.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says the monastery gave more grain in bad years, which implies it also gave grain in other years.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The monastery was buying grain at high prices, which would cost it money, not make it wealthier.

passages.text: Ecologist Mara Lindqvist hung two identical feeders side by side in a meadow. One held a solution that was 20 percent sugar, and the other held a solution that was 10 percent sugar. Hummingbirds visited the 20 percent feeder far more often. The next morning, Lindqvist swapped the solutions between the two feeders, and the hummingbirds switched too, now favoring the feeder on the other side. These results suggest that the hummingbirds chose between the feeders based on ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the position of each feeder in the meadow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: how much sugar each feeder's solution contained.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the color of each feeder.

choices.label: D
choices.text: which feeder they had visited the day before.

content.explanation: On the first day, the birds preferred the feeder with the 20 percent solution. When that solution was moved to the other feeder, the birds moved with it. The one thing that followed the birds' preference was the sugar solution, so the birds were most likely choosing based on how much sugar each feeder held (choice B).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: After the swap, the birds abandoned the position they had favored and went to the other side, so position was not what they were choosing by.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The feeders were identical, so color could not explain why the birds preferred one over the other.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: On the second day the birds switched away from the feeder they had favored the day before, which is the opposite of returning to the same feeder.

passages.text: Astronomers monitoring a distant star found that its brightness dips by the same small amount every 12.4 days, and each dip lasts almost exactly three hours. Dark patches on a star's surface, called starspots, can also dim a star, but starspots form and fade unpredictably and vary in size, so the dimming they cause is irregular in both timing and depth. Because the dips the astronomers recorded are so regular, they are most likely caused by ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: starspots that appear on the star every 12.4 days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a fault in the instruments used to monitor the star.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a single cloud of dust that drifted between the star and Earth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: an object that passes between the star and Earth at regular intervals, such as an orbiting planet.

content.explanation: The text rules out starspots because their dimming is irregular, while the recorded dips repeat on an exact schedule with the same depth and length. Something that passes in front of the star on a fixed cycle, such as a planet completing an orbit every 12.4 days, would block the same amount of light for the same length of time each pass. That is the explanation that fits the regularity (choice D).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says starspots form and fade unpredictably, so they would not appear on a precise 12.4-day schedule.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text suggests the instruments were faulty, and the text's reasoning is about what in space could cause such regular dips.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: A single drifting cloud would dim the star once, not over and over at a fixed interval.

passages.text: Two versions survive of a piano sonata by the nineteenth-century composer Elise Marrow. Scholars have long assumed that the shorter version is an early draft and the longer version her final revision. However, the shorter version contains several notes higher than any that could be played on the piano Marrow owned until 1831, when she bought an instrument with an extended keyboard. The longer version uses none of those notes, and Marrow is not known to have composed for any piano but her own. These details suggest that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the shorter version may have been written after the longer one, not before it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marrow wrote the longer version for a piano that she did not own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: both versions of the sonata were composed after 1831.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow stopped composing for the piano after she bought her new instrument.

content.explanation: Because Marrow composed for her own piano, the high notes in the shorter version point to a date after 1831, when she had the extended keyboard. The longer version fits her older piano, so it could date from before 1831. That reverses the usual assumption: the shorter version may be the later one rather than an early draft (choice A). The word "may" matters, because the evidence makes this likely without proving it.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Marrow is not known to have composed for any piano but her own, and the longer version's notes fit the piano she owned, so nothing suggests a different instrument.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Only the shorter version requires the post-1831 keyboard. The longer version uses no such notes, so nothing shows it was written after 1831.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The shorter version is evidence that she did compose for the new instrument, which contradicts this choice.

passages.text: When the town of Belford began charging shoppers ten cents for each plastic grocery bag, the number of bags handed out at its grocery stores fell by about 80 percent within a year. Economist Lucia Ferraz noticed, however, that over the same period, sales of small plastic trash bags at those stores roughly tripled. A survey found that before the fee, most Belford households had reused their grocery bags to line kitchen trash cans. Ferraz's findings suggest that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the fee had no effect on how many grocery bags shoppers took.

choices.label: B
choices.text: most Belford households stopped lining their trash cans after the fee began.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the fee reduced the town's overall use of plastic bags by less than the drop in grocery bags alone would indicate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Belford's grocery stores raised the price of trash bags to make up for money lost on grocery bags.

content.explanation: Grocery bags fell by about 80 percent, but households had been reusing those bags as trash can liners. When the free liners disappeared, many households bought plastic trash bags instead, and those sales tripled. Some of the plastic saved at the checkout was therefore used again as trash bags, so total plastic bag use fell by less than the 80 percent figure suggests (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Grocery bags handed out fell by about 80 percent, so the fee clearly affected how many bags shoppers took.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Trash bag sales tripled, which suggests households kept lining their trash cans but switched to bought trash bags.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says nothing about the price of trash bags, and a price increase would not explain why sales tripled.

passages.text: An apple grower placed beehives along the edge of one half of her orchard but not the other. Both halves had the same variety of tree, received the same amount of water, and were planted in the same kind of soil. That fall, trees in the half with the beehives produced about 40 percent more apples than trees in the other half. Because apple blossoms must be pollinated to produce fruit, the grower concluded that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the half without beehives had poorer soil.

choices.label: B
choices.text: trees in the half without beehives received too little water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: apple trees produce more fruit when they are planted farther from beehives.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the bees most likely increased the harvest by pollinating more of the blossoms.

content.explanation: The two halves matched in tree variety, water and soil. The only difference was the beehives, and the half with hives produced more apples. Since blossoms need pollination to become fruit, the likely explanation is that the bees pollinated more blossoms in that half (choice D).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The text says both halves were planted in the same kind of soil.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says both halves received the same amount of water.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is the opposite of the result: the trees near the hives produced more apples, not fewer.

passages.text: Researchers studying an old barn used tree rings to date its wooden beams. On several beams the bark was still attached, meaning that the outermost ring beneath it was the last ring the tree grew before it was cut down. On every one of these beams, that outermost ring formed in 1794. Builders in the region at the time typically used timber within a year of felling it, while the wood was still green and easy to shape. The evidence therefore suggests that the barn was most likely built ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: soon after the trees were cut down, around 1794 or 1795.

choices.label: B
choices.text: several decades before 1794.

choices.label: C
choices.text: from beams taken out of a much older building.

choices.label: D
choices.text: by builders who let their timber dry for many years before using it.

content.explanation: The outermost ring under the bark shows when each tree stopped growing, which is when it was cut down: in 1794 for every beam with bark. Builders at the time usually used timber within a year of cutting it. Putting these together, the barn was most likely built shortly after the trees were felled, around 1794 or 1795 (choice A).

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The trees were still growing in 1794, so the beams could not have been used in a barn built decades earlier.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing suggests the beams were reused, and the usual practice described in the text was to build with freshly cut timber.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says builders typically used timber within a year, while it was still green, which contradicts letting it dry for many years.

passages.text: A magazine devoted to growing vegetables at home asked its readers to complete a survey about their gardens. Of the 4,000 readers who responded, 72 percent said they grow tomatoes, and the magazine announced that tomatoes are "the favorite crop of American gardeners." Sociologist Nadia Brennan points out that many people garden only with flowers or ornamental shrubs, and such people are unlikely to read a magazine about vegetables. Brennan's point implies that the magazine's survey ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: shows that tomatoes are not, in fact, the favorite crop of American gardeners.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is not a reliable basis for the magazine's claim about American gardeners in general.

choices.label: C
choices.text: would have found a higher percentage of tomato growers if more readers had responded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: shows that most of the magazine's readers grow flowers rather than vegetables.

content.explanation: Brennan's point is about who answered the survey. The respondents were readers of a vegetable magazine, and gardeners who grow only flowers or shrubs are unlikely to be among them. So the respondents do not represent American gardeners as a whole, and the survey cannot support a claim about all American gardeners (choice B). Notice that this does not prove the claim false; it only means the survey is the wrong evidence for it.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is too strong. A survey that doesn't represent all gardeners can't prove the magazine's claim, but it can't disprove it either.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing in the text suggests that more responses would raise the percentage. Brennan's concern is about which kinds of gardeners were surveyed, not how many.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The respondents were readers of a vegetable magazine, and most said they grow tomatoes, so nothing suggests most readers grow flowers instead.

passages.text: At one fossil site, paleontologists found footprints left by a single species of plant-eating dinosaur. The prints come in two sizes, large and small, and all of them were pressed into the same layer of mud, which hardened within a few days. The trackways run side by side in the same direction, and none of the small prints cross or overlap the large ones. The researchers concluded that the prints were most likely left by ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: two different species that crossed the site years apart.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a single large animal that walked across the mud several times.

choices.label: C
choices.text: young and adult animals of the same species moving together as a group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: small predators following the large animals' trail in order to hunt them.

content.explanation: All the prints belong to one species, so the two sizes most likely reflect younger and older animals. The prints were made within a few days in the same mud, they run side by side in the same direction, and they don't cross. Together these details point to young and adult animals traveling together as a group (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The prints belong to a single species and were made within a few days, not years apart.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: One animal would leave prints of only one size, but the prints come in two sizes.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: All the prints come from a single plant-eating species, so none were left by predators.

passages.text: Botanist Kofi Mensah studied a mountain wildflower that, in the wild, blooms only in springs that follow a long, cold winter. In a greenhouse, he kept groups of plants at near-freezing temperatures for eight weeks and then warmed them. Every plant older than two years bloomed within a month. Plants younger than two years, given exactly the same cold treatment, produced leaves but no flowers. Plants of any age that were never chilled did not bloom at all. Mensah's results suggest that for this species, ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a long period of cold is enough on its own to make a plant bloom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: plants older than two years can bloom without being exposed to cold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cold temperatures prevent young plants from producing leaves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a period of cold is needed for blooming but works only once a plant has reached a certain age.

content.explanation: Two findings must fit together. First, no unchilled plant bloomed, so cold is needed. Second, chilled plants younger than two years still did not bloom, so cold alone is not enough; the plant also has to be old enough. Choice D states both parts: cold is necessary, but it works only for older plants.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Young plants received the same cold treatment and did not bloom, so cold is not enough on its own.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Plants of any age that were never chilled did not bloom, so older plants also need the cold.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The young plants did produce leaves after the cold treatment; they just didn't flower.

passages.text: Using a sound meter, a student measured the noise level on her street at the same time each evening for two weeks. The amount of traffic on the street stayed about the same throughout. On the one evening after a heavy snowfall, when fresh snow covered the ground and rooftops, the street was noticeably quieter than on any other evening. Fresh snow is full of tiny air pockets that absorb sound waves. The student's measurements therefore suggest that ______

content.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the fresh snow likely absorbed much of the sound on the street.

choices.label: B
choices.text: there was much less traffic on the street that evening.

choices.label: C
choices.text: her sound meter stopped working properly in the cold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: snow makes sound travel farther than usual.

content.explanation: Traffic stayed about the same, so the amount of noise being made didn't change much. The one difference on the quiet evening was the fresh snow, and the text says fresh snow absorbs sound waves. So the snow most likely absorbed much of the sound (choice A).

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The text says traffic stayed about the same throughout the two weeks.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Nothing suggests the meter malfunctioned, and the text offers a direct explanation for the quieter reading: snow absorbs sound.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The text says snow absorbs sound, which would make the street quieter, not carry sound farther.
